analysis.one_liner: Taxes stock and futures trades to make Wall Street repay the cost of its 2008 bailout.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from February 2009 until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a tax of up to 0.25% on trades of stocks, options, futures, and other financial instruments, paid by the exchanges where the trades happen. The tax would be sized to raise enough money to repay the federal government's net cost of the 2008 bank bailout (TARP) and Federal Reserve emergency lending, and it would phase out once that cost was recouped. The sponsor argued the tax would barely touch ordinary retirement investors and would fall mainly on high-volume traders. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, if the tax succeeded in recovering the public cost of the bank bailout from the financial industry rather than the general Treasury; the bill's findings say a 0.25% tax could raise roughly $150 billion a year, far more than TARP's net cost would require, with the excess allowed only while the net bailout cost remains unrecovered.

how_it_helps.text: The tax would be set at whatever percentage up to 0.25% is needed to recoup the net federal cost of TARP and Federal Reserve bailout lending, and would phase out once that cost is repaid.

The bill places the tax on securities and commodities transactions, paid by the trading facility, so the cost falls on the markets that were stabilized by the bailout rather than on the general taxpayer.
The bill's findings state that a securities transfer tax has a negligible impact on the average investor, and note the United States imposed a similar stock transfer tax from 1914 to 1966.

analysis.who_pays: High-frequency traders, brokerages, and the financial industry, which would pay the tax on each transaction; some of that cost could be passed to institutional and active retail traders, and critics of transaction taxes generally argue they can reduce market liquidity and slightly raise trading costs.

drawbacks.text: Transaction taxes of this kind are typically passed through to trading costs, so even investors who do not day-trade could pay somewhat more through fund expenses and wider spreads; the bill's own mechanism taxes every covered transaction, not only large institutional trades.
The tax is charged on both sale and purchase of covered instruments, so round-trip trades would pay the percentage twice, and exchanges paying the tax would likely recover it from their customers.
The tax rate would be set by the Treasury Secretary's estimate of TARP and Federal Reserve costs, so the final rate would depend on administrative judgment rather than a fixed figure set by statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear: shifting the cost of a Wall Street bailout from general taxpayers to the traders who benefited. The design is reasonable in that it is capped at 0.25%, expires once the bailout is repaid, and follows a transfer tax the U.S. used for over fifty years; the main honest cost is that high-frequency trading costs would rise and some of that could reach ordinary investors indirectly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Peter DeFazio and seven colleagues introduced the bill on February 13, 2009.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill expired with the 111th Congress in January 2011.
Thirteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill, all within DeFazio's own party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-volume trading firms, banks, and the financial industry, which avoided paying a transaction tax that could have raised roughly $150 billion a year and instead left the bailout's net cost with general taxpayers; the Ways and Means Committee also gained by not having to take a position on it.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eight original cosponsors.

for.name: 13 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Welch, Sutton, Capuano, Wu, Stark, DeLauro, and Edwards among the original cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Charles Rangel (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, marked up, or reported the bill after referral; no action appears in its record.

against.name: Financial industry
against.role: Securities exchanges, banks, and trading firms that would have paid the tax
against.what_they_did: The record shows no activity by the industry, and the bill generated no committee action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill, but it never reached a vote, so the actual partisan split is unknown; no House Republican is recorded as taking any position on it.

industries.note: The bill puts the tax directly on trading facilities and, by extension, on high-volume traders. They avoided it when the bill died, keeping transaction costs at zero and leaving TARP's net cost with the general taxpayer.

As parties that were stabilized by TARP and Federal Reserve emergency lending, they would have effectively repaid the public cost of their own rescue through the tax. The bill's failure left that cost with taxpayers.

The bill's findings argue the tax barely touches average investors, but every covered trade is taxed, so fund and brokerage costs could rise slightly. The direct benefit to them is that bailout costs come off the general taxpayer ledger.
